BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- The U.S. military formally handed authority over Baghdad's "Green Zone" to Iraqis on Thursday as new pacts governing the mission of international troops replaced a U.N. mandate. An Iraqi honor guard parades outside the former palace of Saddam Hussein in Baghdad on Thursday. Iraqi troops took over checkpoints around the heavily protected district, formally known as the International Zone, which houses Iraqi government offices and the U.S. Embassy. Saddam Hussein's Republican Palace, which served as U.S. headquarters in Baghdad after the 2003 invasion that ousted Iraq's longtime strongman, was among the facilities handed over in Thursday's ceremony. "This day is a great day in the history of the Iraqi people," Iraqi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta said. Maj. Gen. David Perkins, a U.S. military spokesman, noted the significance of turning over the former Republican Palace.  Watch what goes on in the "Green Zone" » . "The palace was handed back to the Iraqi people, significant as symbol of the head of the government and a sign for increased sovereignty," he said at a news conference with Atta. Thursday marked the first day of a U.S.-Iraqi pact that allows U.S. forces to remain in the country until 2011, under tighter restrictions. Similar agreements have been signed with other coalition countries that remain in Iraq. A U.N. mandate that authorized international forces in the country expired Wednesday. Perkins said American troops will continue to fight alongside Iraqis -- "but the Iraqis will be in the lead." "When you come up to a checkpoint, the Iraqis will check your identification. They will make the decision if you come in or go out," he said. "We will continue to be there to provide some technical capacity, to provide some mentoring, but you will see less and less American forces and more and more Iraqi forces -- and they will have the majority of the responsibility for making those key decisions which determine the security of the capital." Iraq's three-member Presidency Council ratified the new pact in December. Under the deal, U.S. troops will withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, and all American troops will leave the country by the end of 2011, more than eight years after the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Hussein. The agreement authorizes the "temporary assistance" of U.S. forces but severely restricts their role. It requires Iraqi approval for all military operations and gives Iraqi courts the right to try U.S. troops and contractors for "grave premeditated felonies."

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) —** The U.S. military formally transferred authority over Baghdad’s “Green Zone” to Iraqis on Thursday, as new agreements governing the mission of international troops replaced a U.N. mandate.

An Iraqi honor guard paraded outside Saddam Hussein’s former palace in Baghdad on Thursday. Iraqi troops assumed control of checkpoints around the heavily protected district, formally known as the International Zone, which houses Iraqi government offices and the U.S. Embassy.

Saddam Hussein’s Republican Palace, which served as the U.S. headquarters in Baghdad following the 2003 invasion that ousted Iraq’s longtime strongman, was among the facilities transferred during Thursday’s ceremony.

“This day is a great day in the history of the Iraqi people,” Iraqi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta said.

Maj. Gen. David Perkins, a U.S. military spokesman, emphasized the significance of returning the former Republican Palace to Iraqi control.

“The palace was handed back to the Iraqi people, significant as a symbol of the head of the government and a sign of increased sovereignty,” he said at a news conference with Atta.

*Watch what goes on in the “Green Zone” »*

Thursday marked the first day of a U.S.-Iraqi agreement allowing U.S. forces to remain in the country until 2011, subject to tighter restrictions. Similar agreements have been signed with other coalition countries that continue to have troops in Iraq. A U.N. mandate authorizing international forces in the country expired Wednesday.

Perkins said American troops would continue to fight alongside Iraqi forces, “but the Iraqis will be in the lead.”

“When you come up to a checkpoint, the Iraqis will check your identification. They will make the decision if you come in or go out,” he said. “We will continue to be there to provide some technical capacity, to provide some mentoring, but you will see less and less American forces and more and more Iraqi forces—and they will have the majority of the responsibility for making those key decisions which determine the security of the capital.”

Iraq’s three-member Presidency Council ratified the new agreement in December. Under the deal, U.S. troops will withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, and all American troops will leave the country by the end of 2011—more than eight years after the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Hussein.

The agreement authorizes the “temporary assistance” of U.S. forces but sharply restricts their role. It requires Iraqi approval for all military operations and grants Iraqi courts the right to try U.S. troops and contractors for “grave premeditated felonies.”

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) —** Iraq assumed formal control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone on Thursday, the same day new agreements regulating foreign military operations replaced an expired United Nations mandate.

Iraqi soldiers began staffing checkpoints surrounding the district, officially called the International Zone, where the U.S. Embassy and Iraqi government offices are located. An Iraqi honor guard also marched outside Saddam Hussein’s former palace during the handover ceremony.

The Republican Palace was among the sites transferred to Iraqi authority. After the U.S.-led 2003 invasion removed longtime ruler Saddam Hussein, the building became the American military’s headquarters in Baghdad.

Iraqi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta described the occasion as “a great day in the history of the Iraqi people.”

At a joint news conference with Atta, U.S. military spokesman Maj. Gen. David Perkins emphasized the symbolic importance of returning the palace.

“The palace was handed back to the Iraqi people, significant as symbol of the head of the government and a sign for increased sovereignty,” Perkins said.

**Watch what happens inside the “Green Zone” »**

Thursday was also the first day of a new U.S.-Iraqi security agreement permitting American forces to stay in Iraq through 2011, although under stricter limits. Other coalition nations still operating in Iraq have entered into similar arrangements. The previous U.N. authorization for international troops expired on Wednesday.

Perkins said U.S. forces would continue combat operations alongside Iraqi troops, but that Iraqi personnel would take the leading role.

According to Perkins, Iraqi forces would inspect identification and decide who could enter or leave at checkpoints. American troops would remain available to offer technical support and guidance, but their presence would gradually decrease as Iraqi forces assumed greater responsibility for crucial decisions affecting security in the capital.

Iraq’s three-member Presidency Council approved the agreement in December. It requires U.S. forces to leave Iraqi cities and towns by June 30 and mandates the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq by the end of 2011—more than eight years after the invasion that overthrew Hussein.

Although the pact permits U.S. forces to provide “temporary assistance,” it places major constraints on their activities. Every military operation must receive Iraqi authorization, and Iraqi courts may prosecute American troops and contractors accused of “grave premeditated felonies.”

The United States military transferred formal control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone to Iraqi security forces as a United Nations mandate authorizing the presence of international troops expired and new bilateral agreements took effect.

The handover marked a major symbolic step in Iraq’s effort to regain full control over its territory and security institutions. The Green Zone, which includes Iraqi government offices, diplomatic missions and other key facilities, had been guarded primarily by U.S.-led forces since the 2003 invasion. Its concrete barriers, armed checkpoints and tightly controlled entrances made it one of the most secure areas in the capital.

Under the new arrangements, Iraqi troops assumed primary responsibility for protecting the district, staffing checkpoints and regulating access. U.S. forces remained available to provide training, advice and operational support but moved away from their former front-line security role.

The transition followed the expiration of the U.N. mandate that had provided the legal basis for coalition military operations in Iraq. In its place, agreements negotiated between Washington and Baghdad established new rules for the temporary presence and activities of American forces, while recognizing the Iraqi government’s expanding authority.

Iraqi officials presented the transfer as evidence that the country’s security forces were increasingly capable of protecting important institutions and maintaining order. For the United States, it represented a shift from direct control toward a supporting and mentoring role.

Although American personnel continued to operate in and around the Green Zone, day-to-day security became an Iraqi responsibility. The handover was therefore both practical and symbolic, signaling a broader transition toward greater Iraqi sovereignty and eventual full control over national security.

# Iraq takes control of Saddam’s former palace as Green Zone transition begins

**BAGHDAD, Iraq — January 1, 2009** — Iraq formally took control of Saddam Hussein’s former Republican Palace on Thursday, a highly symbolic handover that coincided with a broader transfer of security authority in Baghdad’s fortified Green Zone and the start of a timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. forces.

The sprawling palace complex, once a monument to Saddam’s rule and later the center of the American presence in Iraq, was returned to the Iraqi government as a new U.S.-Iraq security agreement took effect.

For years, the building had housed the U.S. Embassy and offices connected to the American-led administration established after the 2003 invasion. Its return was intended to demonstrate that Iraq was reclaiming both sovereign territory and responsibility for institutions that had remained under U.S. control.

“This palace is a symbol of Iraqi sovereignty,” Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki said during ceremonies marking the transition, presenting the handover as evidence that the country was moving beyond occupation and toward full control of its affairs.

## A powerful symbol changes hands

Built on the banks of the Tigris River, the Republican Palace was one of the most visible expressions of Saddam’s power. After U.S.-led forces entered Baghdad in April 2003, the complex became headquarters for the Coalition Provisional Authority, which governed Iraq until sovereignty was formally transferred to an interim Iraqi administration in June 2004.

The palace later served as the U.S. Embassy, even as Iraqi officials operated from other buildings inside the Green Zone.

Its handover became possible after the United States moved diplomatic operations to a new, heavily fortified embassy compound nearby. The new facility was designed to house American diplomats and support staff without relying on the former presidential complex.

Although the transfer was ceremonial as well as practical, Iraqi officials described it as an important step in reversing the physical legacy of the invasion.

## Green Zone security shifts to Iraqi control

The transition also extended beyond the palace.

Iraqi forces assumed greater responsibility for security in the International Zone, commonly known as the Green Zone, the heavily protected district that contains government ministries, parliament, foreign embassies and residences used by senior officials.

The area had been administered and guarded primarily by U.S.-led forces since 2003. Concrete barriers, checkpoints and razor wire turned the district into one of the most fortified sections of Baghdad, separating it from neighborhoods that endured some of the worst violence of the war.

Under the new arrangement, Iraqi troops and police took the lead at checkpoints and around key government buildings. U.S. forces remained available to provide support during the transition, and American personnel continued to maintain security around U.S. diplomatic facilities.

The shift did not mean that the Green Zone suddenly lost its extensive defenses. Rather, responsibility for operating them moved increasingly to Iraqi authorities.

The transfer was closely watched because the Green Zone had repeatedly been targeted by rocket and mortar attacks. Iraqi officials said their security forces were prepared to assume control, but U.S. commanders acknowledged that the process would require coordination and continued assistance.

## Security agreement replaces U.N. mandate

The changes followed the expiration of the United Nations mandate that had provided the legal basis for the presence of U.S.-led coalition forces in Iraq.

In its place, Washington and Baghdad negotiated two agreements: a broader framework for long-term cooperation and a security pact governing the temporary presence and activities of U.S. forces.

The security accord, often referred to as the Status of Forces Agreement, established deadlines for the withdrawal of American troops and placed new restrictions on U.S. military operations.

Among its provisions:

- U.S. combat forces were required to leave Iraqi cities, towns and villages by **June 30, 2009**.
- All U.S. forces were to withdraw from Iraq by **December 31, 2011**.
- American military operations were to be coordinated with the Iraqi government.
- Iraqi authorities gained greater control over detentions and the handling of prisoners.
- Iraq received increased legal authority over U.S. personnel and contractors in specified circumstances.

The agreement had been approved by Iraq’s parliament after months of difficult negotiations. Its supporters said it provided a clear path toward ending the foreign military presence while avoiding a sudden security vacuum.

Critics in Iraq argued that the timetable allowed U.S. troops to remain too long or left too much ambiguity about military operations. Others worried that Iraqi forces might not be ready to operate without extensive American support.

## Withdrawal to occur in stages

The June 2009 deadline required U.S. troops to pull back from populated areas and consolidate at bases outside cities. Iraqi security forces were expected to take primary responsibility for day-to-day operations in Baghdad, Mosul and other urban centers.

The second deadline, at the end of 2011, called for the departure of all remaining U.S. forces unless the two governments negotiated a new arrangement.

The timetable did not require every American service member to leave immediately after the palace handover. At the beginning of 2009, roughly 140,000 U.S. troops remained in Iraq, and commanders planned a phased reduction shaped by security conditions, logistical requirements and policy decisions by the incoming administration of President-elect Barack Obama.

Obama had campaigned on ending the Iraq war and withdrawing combat forces, though he also said the pace would have to account for military advice and conditions on the ground. The bilateral agreement negotiated under President George W. Bush set the legal outer limit for the U.S. military presence.

American officials stressed that the withdrawal deadlines applied to military forces, not to ordinary diplomatic relations. The United States intended to retain a large embassy and continue providing political, economic and security assistance to Iraq.

## Questions remain over Iraqi readiness

The handover came after a significant decline in violence from the levels seen during the sectarian conflict of 2006 and 2007. U.S. and Iraqi officials credited several factors, including the deployment of additional American troops, cooperation with Sunni tribal groups, offensives by Iraqi forces and the weakening of al Qaeda in Iraq.

But the security situation remained fragile. Insurgent bombings continued, political disputes persisted among Iraq’s Shiite, Sunni Arab and Kurdish communities, and concerns remained about the capabilities and political neutrality of Iraqi security forces.

The transfer of the Green Zone therefore represented both a statement of confidence and a test.

For Iraqi leaders, the palace ceremony offered a potent image: a building once controlled by Saddam, then by the American occupation administration, was again in Iraqi hands.

For the United States, the moment marked the beginning of a new phase — one in which its military would move from a dominant role toward withdrawal, while its diplomats attempted to build a more conventional relationship with an increasingly sovereign Iraqi government.

The palace handover did not end the war, nor did it immediately remove the walls and checkpoints that had come to define central Baghdad. But it placed a visible Iraqi stamp on the seat of government and started the clock on a withdrawal timetable that called for the U.S. military presence to end within three years.
